variants.name: boost::base_from_member (Boost.Utility)
variants.idiom_name: boost::base_from_member<MemberType, UniqueID> as a private base
variants.implementation_notes: C++ is the pattern's home because the order is fixed by the language: virtual bases, then direct bases left to right as they appear in the base-specifier list, then non-static data members in declaration order - so the derived class controls when a helper base is constructed simply by where it puts it. The library form is boost/utility/base_from_member.hpp: a class template with a protected member named member, constructed by a single variadic constructor template that perfect-forwards its arguments (constexpr and with propagated noexcept on C++11 and later), plus a specialisation for MemberType& that binds a reference; on pre-C++11 compilers the same header supplies a default constructor and up to BOOST_BASE_FROM_MEMBER_MAX_ARITY (10) constructor templates. Inherit it privately and first, construct it from the arguments, and pass member (or its address) to the base that needs it - and use the second template parameter, the int UniqueID, when two subobjects of the same member type are required, because a class cannot have two direct bases of one type. Keep the inheritance private: the Boost documentation states the idiom is an implementation detail and should not be visible to clients or derived classes.
pitfalls: The base-specifier list is load order: inserting another base before the base_from_member entry, or reordering the list for style, constructs std::ostream first and reinstates undefined behaviour without any compiler diagnostic.

Two base_from_member subobjects of the same member type need distinct UniqueID tags; without one the second is a repeated base class and the program is ill-formed (base classes are unnamed, so a class cannot have two direct bases of the same type).
Making the helper public or protected exposes both member and a base_from_member base in the class's interface; the Boost documentation is explicit that this idiom stays private.

The constructor template cannot be told which template parameters to use, so arguments must already be close to the member's intended constructor type - explicit conversions may be needed, and a non-copyable member silently makes the whole class non-copyable.

variants.name: Hand-written holder base (pbase) for pre-C++11 or non-Boost code
variants.idiom_name: custom struct fdostream_pbase { fdoutbuf sbuffer; ... } inherited first
variants.implementation_notes: The bare form of the idiom, shown in the Wikibooks chapter and endorsed by the Boost documentation ('manually coding a base class may be better if the construction and/or copying needs are too complex for the supplied template class'): write a small struct whose only member is the based-member, give it a constructor that initialises the member from whatever arguments it needs, and inherit it privately and first. There is no dependency on Boost and no template machinery; the derived class names the holder explicitly in its member-initialiser list and passes the member (or its address) to the dependent base. Choose it when the member's construction does more than forward arguments, when the holder must expose accessors or non-copyable semantics of its own, or when a third-party dependency is not acceptable; choose the library template when several holders of one type or a reference member make boilerplate multiply.
pitfalls: The holder is a per-type struct: every member type needs its own holder, and two holders of identical shape cannot substitute for one another, so repeated members of one type need distinct holder types where the library template would take a tag.
Nothing in the holder records that another base depends on it: a later cleanup that turns the holder back into a plain member, or that reorders the base list, breaks the object silently.

Copy and move semantics follow the member: a non-copyable member (buffer, mutex, reference) makes the class non-copyable unless the holder's special members are written deliberately - and a reference member must be initialised in the holder's constructor.
